name: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
title: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
answer: Agentic drafting and multi-model workflows describe a way of writing in which a language model is given a role, a goal and a set of tools, then allowed to act across several steps rather than answer once. In literary work the agent might outline a chapter, draft a scene, critique its own draft, and revise, while different models handle different jobs such as prose, continuity checking or research. The practice sits inside narrative design because the writer is still shaping voice, structure and meaning, and the agent is a collaborator that can be directed, interrupted and overruled. It is less a single technique than a way of arranging several models and prompts into a working pipeline.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The setup usually runs on a chat interface or an API, with the writer's own manuscript, notes and style guide supplied as context. Multi-model work means routing tasks between systems, for example one model for long-form drafting, another for editing or fact-checking, and a third for structured output such as scene beats or character sheets. Some writers keep everything in a single hosted service, others connect tools through scripts or orchestration frameworks that pass text and instructions between models. Local models are an option when a manuscript must stay off external servers, though they demand more hardware and patience.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a brief: premise, point of view, tense, target length and the constraints a scene must satisfy. The writer then assigns the agent a role, gives it the relevant excerpt and asks for a draft, a set of alternatives or a critique, reviewing output at each step instead of accepting a whole chapter at once. Multi-model workflows split these jobs deliberately, sending structural questions to one model and line-level prose to another, then reconciling the results by hand. Continuity is tracked through running notes, character bibles and summaries that are fed back into later prompts. The writer remains the editor, deciding what survives.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance matter because the origin of every sentence affects copyright, contracts and disclosure. Publishers and magazines increasingly ask whether and how generative tools were used, and some contracts require a writer to warrant that the work is their own. Training data and model terms vary, so what a model can lawfully reproduce or how output may be used is not uniform, and this is a matter for a lawyer rather than a rule of thumb. Keeping drafts, prompts and version history is the practical way to show how a text was made. Attribution conventions for AI-assisted writing are still forming, and practices differ between genres and markets.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward longer, more autonomous runs in which an agent plans a sequence of drafting and revision tasks and reports back, with the writer supervising rather than prompting each step. Better memory and retrieval should let a model hold a whole novel's continuity without constant reminders, and evaluation tools may help writers compare model outputs against a stated style. Expect more standardised disclosure norms and clearer contractual language around AI assistance. The craft question will stay the same: whether the pipeline serves the voice, or the voice gets flattened to fit the pipeline.
